sections.title: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

summary.text: Summarises the report, explaining that HSV2 is the main cause of genital ulcer disease, is very common where HIV epidemics are severe, and may facilitate HIV transmission in a two-way interaction. It notes that the workshop reviewed evidence and set priorities across epidemiology, HSV2–HIV interaction, therapy, vaccines and behavioural and microbicide studies.

sections.extract: Herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV2) infection is the primary cause of genital herpes. It is highly prevalent in human populations in many parts of the world, and is the most common cause of genital ulcer disease worldwide. In developing countries, the major public health importance of HSV2 relates to its potential role in facilitating HIV transmission. HSV2 is highly prevalent in most regions experiencing severe HIV

sections.title: INTRODUCTION

summary.text: Introduces the workshop by setting out the public health importance of HSV2 in developing countries and its suspected role in HIV spread. It explains that experts from developing and industrialized countries were invited to consider control measures.

sections.title: OBJECTIVES

summary.text: States the workshop's objectives: to review knowledge on HSV2 epidemiology, its interaction with HIV, control measures and diagnostics, to identify knowledge gaps, and to set research and programme priorities.

sections.extract: 1. To review existing knowledge in the following four areas, with a particular focus on developing countries: ■The epidemiology and natural history of HSV2 ■The interaction between HSV2 and HIV ■HSV2 control measures ■HSV2 diagnostics. 2.To identify important gaps in knowledge in each of these areas requiring further study. 3.To establish priorities for future research and control programmes. 2. sections.title: PARTICIPANTS AND METHODOLOGY

summary.text: Describes the 40 participants and the workshop's format of presentations, breakout groups and plenary prioritisation. It then reviews the epidemiology and natural history of HSV2, including rising prevalence worldwide and its role as the leading cause of genital ulcer disease. Table 1 gives seroprevalence figures for general populations in Africa, Latin America and Asia, and the section discusses HSV2 as a marker of sexual behaviour. It ends with recommended studies, including of discordant couples, with attention to counselling and treatment.

sections.extract: Forty participants attended the workshop (Annex 1), and areas of expertise included virology, epidemiology, surveillance, behavioural science, clinical medicine, mathematical modelling and STI programme development and implementation in developing countries. Participants came from Africa (10),Asia (1), Europe (18) and North America (7). In addition, three representatives of UN agencies were present, and one from

sections.title: Biological and clinical research

summary.text: Explains the two-way biological interaction between HIV and HSV2, with HIV increasing HSV2 reactivation, shedding and severity, and HSV2 lesions containing HIV. It notes some evidence that aciclovir may prolong survival in people with HIV.

sections.extract: HIV and HSV2 manifest a bi-directional interaction. HSV2 increases the efficiency of HIV acquisition and transmission whereas HIV may increase susceptibility to HSV2 and increase HSV2 shedding, HSV2 recurrence rate and severity of clinical manifestations. EFFECT OF HIV INFECTION ON NATURAL HISTORY OF HSV2 HSV2 reactivation and duration of recurrences are significantly increased in HIV infected individuals

sections.title: INTERACTION BETWEEN HSV2 AND HIV

summary.text: Continues the review of how HSV2 may increase HIV shedding, noting that aciclovir lowers both viruses in lesions and that data from developing countries are lacking. It lists recommended biological studies, such as whether the effect differs in Africa because of co-infections.

sections.title: Epidemiological research

summary.text: Summarises epidemiological evidence that HSV2 raises the risk of acquiring HIV, from a meta-analysis showing about a two-fold risk in men and weaker findings in women. It discusses why cross-sectional studies show stronger associations and recommends prospective studies and estimates of population attributable fractions.

sections.title: Genital ulcer disease in Africa: Epidemiological trends

summary.text: Describes changes in the causes of genital ulcer disease in Africa, with Table 2 showing herpes rising and chancroid and syphilis falling at a South African mine clinic from 1986 to 1998. It notes that this undermines syndromic management and recommends monitoring ulcer causes by sex, HIV status and risk group.

sections.extract: Chancroid, syphilis and genital herpes are all common causes of genital ulcer disease (GUD) in developing countries. However, there is some evidence that there have been changes in the aetiology of GUD in recent years [O’Farrell, 1999], and this may influence the appropriateness of current syndromic management. sections.title: HSV2 CONTROL MEASURES FOR DEVELOPING COUNTRIES
Case management of HSV2 in areas of Africa with high HIV prevalence

summary.text: Explains why clinical diagnosis of genital ulcers is unreliable where HIV is common and why rising herpes cases may increase syndromic treatment failure. It recommends lobbying for affordable aciclovir, evaluating its addition to syndromic algorithms, and strengthening health education.

sections.title: The role of episodic and suppressive therapy in HSV2 and HIV control

summary.text: Compares episodic and suppressive therapy for genital herpes with aciclovir, valaciclovir and famciclovir, summarising their effects on symptoms, shedding and recurrences. It considers how such therapy might reduce HIV transmission or acquisition. It recommends randomised trials in high-risk groups, such as serodiscordant couples and sex workers, with monitoring for drug resistance.

sections.extract: IN HSV2 AND HIV CONTROL Two main treatment strategies are possible for herpes: episodic and suppressive treatment. ■Episodic therapy: ➔Treatment of primary genital herpes ➔Treatment of recurrent genital herpes ■Suppressive therapy: ➔To prevent recurrences. Aciclovir is an antiviral drug, which has been the standard treatment for genital herpes for the past decade in developed countries.Two new therapeutic agents

sections.title: Vaccine trials

summary.text: Discusses prophylactic and therapeutic HSV2 vaccines, the immune responses they should induce and the results of recent candidate vaccine trials. It considers how vaccine trials could be designed in developing countries, with HSV2 disease as the main endpoint and HIV infection as a secondary one.

sections.extract: Given the high prevalence of HSV2 infection in many countries, and the fact that most infections are subclinical, the development of an effective HSV2 vaccine would provide a powerful control tool. HSV2 vaccines can be divided into two main categories according to whether they target infected or uninfected individuals. Prophylactic vaccines: aim at protecting against HSV infection or disease in the uninfected

sections.title: Other preventive strategies

summary.text: Reviews other HSV2 prevention strategies where vaccines and therapy are not feasible, including behavioural interventions, condoms and female-controlled methods such as microbicides. It also covers counselling and states that widespread HSV2 screening was not recommended at that stage.

sections.extract: In the absence of a vaccine or feasible therapeutic strategy in many developing countries, other preventive strategies are needed for HSV2 (and HIV) control. Discussions focused on female-controlled methods and behavioural interventions. summary.text: Describes how mathematical modelling has been used to understand HSV2 spread and its interaction with HIV, and summarises findings on antiviral treatment and behaviour change. It lists further modelling needs, such as drug resistance, cost-effectiveness and vaccine effects.

sections.title: HSV2 DIAGNOSIS

summary.text: Reviews HSV2 diagnostic methods, including gold-standard Western blot, commercial ELISA tests, ways to measure incidence, and PCR detection of viral shedding. It lists research needs, such as evaluating assays on African sera and developing rapid tests for herpetic ulcers.

sections.extract: Evaluation of HSV2 assays is based on sensitivity, specificity and reproducibility, and independent blinded comparison. summary.text: Introduces the agreed research and control priorities, starting with epidemiology and natural history, such as testing stored and sentinel surveillance sera for HSV2 prevalence and using cohort data to study the effect of HSV2 on HIV acquisition by sex and age.

sections.title: Biological studies: HSV2 and its interaction with HIV

summary.text: Sets out the priority for clinical studies of how subclinical HSV2 shedding affects HIV shedding and transmission, ideally in areas with high rates of both infections.

sections.extract: ■Clinical studies to assess the effect of subclinical HSV2 infection on HIV shedding There is strong evidence of the bi-directional interaction between HIV and HSV2 in co- infected subjects. However, there is insufficient evidence concerning the effect of asymptomatic HSV2 shedding on HIV transmission. Studies of HIV shedding in HSV2- infected subjects, and of the relative importance of unrecognized HSV2 infection

sections.title: Episodic and suppressive therapy

summary.text: Lists treatment-related priorities, including monitoring the causes of genital ulcers in clinic attenders by sex and HIV status, assessing aciclovir in syndromic management, and studying the effect of episodic therapy on HIV shedding. It also calls for randomised trials of suppressive therapy to prevent HIV in high-risk groups.

sections.extract: ■Monitoring GUD aetiology in STI clinic attenders by gender and HIV status Changes in the aetiology of GUD in some countries has been associated with an increase in the frequency of treatment failure when using the syndromic approach to diagnose and treat STIs. sections.title: Vaccination

summary.text: Proposes a working group to engage vaccine companies, lobby for prophylactic vaccine development and affordability in developing countries, and advance the DISC vaccine to later-phase trials.

sections.extract: It was agreed to form a working group to establish a dialogue with commercial companies involved in HSV2 vaccine development and production.The group should engage these companies in discussions regarding further development and testing of the two types of HSV2 vaccine, prophylactic and therapeutic. sections.title: Behavioural and microbicide studies

summary.text: Lists behavioural and microbicide priorities, including continued promotion of behaviour change and condoms, evaluation of HSV2 counselling and clinic management of herpes, and including HSV2 as an outcome in microbicide trials.

sections.title: Mathematical modelling

summary.text: Recommends further modelling of HSV2 transmission and control, drug resistance, the cost-effectiveness of treatment strategies and the effects of vaccination on HIV.

summary.text: Lists diagnostic priorities: rapid tests for herpes ulcers to guide syndromic management, and evaluation of serological tests on African sera.
